comp_013:n1.prompt:
You are helping me prepare to scope this year's annual penetration test and shortlist candidate firms. I will need to make the final vendor selection myself, so your job is research and drafting only.

First, ask me for any details you need that aren't already obvious from our environment, such as: our domain, the systems/apps in scope (web app, APIs, cloud infra, internal network, mobile app), our cloud provider(s), the compliance driver (SOC 2, customer requirement, etc.), our target testing window, and our budget range if I have one.

Then:
1. Draft a scoping document covering: in-scope assets/domains/IP ranges, out-of-scope items, test type (black-box/gray-box/white-box), testing methodology expected (e.g. OWASP, NIST-based), timeline, and any compliance language SOC 2 auditors typically expect (e.g. reference to a recognized methodology, named tester, dated report, retest confirmation).
2. Research and shortlist 4-6 reputable penetration-testing firms that fit our scope and budget, checking for relevant certifications (e.g. OSCP-certified testers, CREST membership), SOC 2 experience, industry reviews, and sample report availability. For each, summarize services offered, typical turnaround time, certifications, and any pricing information you can find publicly.
3. Prepare a comparison table (firm, certifications, experience with our stack/compliance need, turnaround, estimated cost, notable pros/cons) and a short list of questions to ask each firm (e.g. retest policy, report format, insurance/liability).

Do not contact vendors, sign anything, or make the final selection — this remains a human step. When done, give me the scoping document draft, the firm comparison table, and the question list, then stop for human sign-off so I can pick the firm and proceed to rules-of-engagement authorization myself.

comp_013:n2.prompt:
You are helping me prepare (but not sign) the Rules of Engagement (RoE) authorization for our annual penetration test. This document grants the pen test firm legal permission to attack our systems, so it must be signed by an authorized company officer — you cannot sign it for me.

First, ask me for anything missing: (1) the name of the pen test firm we've engaged, (2) the agreed test dates/window, (3) the in-scope systems, domains, IP ranges, and applications, (4) explicitly out-of-scope systems, (5) permitted testing techniques (e.g., social engineering, DoS testing) and any exclusions, (6) emergency contacts on both sides and escalation/stop-work procedure, (7) data handling rules for any sensitive data encountered, (8) the name and title of the officer who will sign, and (9) any draft RoE document or template the firm already sent us.

Using these inputs, draft or fill in the complete RoE document covering: scope, timing, authorized techniques, exclusions, emergency contacts, escalation procedure, data handling, confidentiality terms, and signature blocks for both parties. Also prepare a short cover checklist summarizing key terms (scope, dates, contacts) for the officer to review before signing, and note where an e-signature tool would be used if we have one configured.

Done looks like: a complete, reviewed RoE draft plus checklist ready for the officer's review, with all placeholders filled in and no open questions remaining.

Do not sign, execute, or submit the RoE on my behalf, and do not use any e-signature tool to finalize it. Once the draft and checklist are ready, stop for human sign-off and report back with the finished document, the checklist, and a list of any assumptions you made.

comp_013:n3.prompt:
You are helping me provision the test environment and accounts for our annual penetration test. This is step n3 of the pen test process: the scope and rules-of-engagement should already be agreed with the testing firm; now we need to hand them a working, isolated environment with appropriate access.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available in our systems or configured credentials: (1) the agreed scope document or summary (which apps/systems/environments are in-scope, e.g. staging vs a dedicated test copy), (2) the testing firm's contact(s) who need accounts, (3) the target test window dates, and (4) whether we're providing a cloned/staging environment or carving out access in production.

Then, using your configured credentials, take these actions:
- Verify or create an isolated test environment that mirrors production closely enough to be meaningful but does not risk live customer data (use a staging environment, a sanitized/synthetic-data clone, or a dedicated test tenant, per what's agreed in scope).
- Create scoped, time-limited accounts for the testing firm's named testers with only the access levels the rules-of-engagement specify (e.g. standard user, admin, or API access) — avoid granting broader permissions than agreed.
- Confirm network/firewall or allow-list rules are updated if the testers need to reach the environment from specific IP ranges.
- Document each account created (username, role/permission level, expiry date) and the environment details (URL, version, what data it contains) in a short handoff note.
- Set a calendar reminder or task to revoke/deactivate these accounts and decommission the test environment immediately after the test window closes.

Done looks like: the testing firm has working credentials and reachable access to a properly scoped, isolated test environment, and you have a written handoff note listing accounts, permissions, expiry, and environment details.

Report back with: the handoff note, confirmation of what was provisioned, any access or environment issues you couldn't resolve, and the date you've scheduled for account teardown.

comp_013:n4.prompt:
You are helping me track the 'testing window' phase of our annual penetration test. This is the period where our external pen-test firm actively runs their attacks against our environment on their own schedule — the actual testing execution remains a human step (performed by the third-party firm, not us) and cannot be done or accelerated from our side.

Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: the pen-test firm's name, the agreed testing window start and end dates (from the rules-of-engagement document), the primary point of contact at the firm, and where we track engagement status internally (e.g., a ticket, project doc, or tracker link).
2. Create or update a tracking entry/checklist item noting: firm name, scope reference, window start/end dates, contact info, and a note that this is a passive monitoring period — we are waiting on the firm, not acting.
3. Prepare a short status-check message I can send to the firm's contact near the window's end date, asking for confirmation that testing is complete and an estimated timeline for the findings report. Draft this but do not send it — that decision is mine.
4. Set a reminder/checkpoint (note it in the tracker) for the window's end date so I know to follow up if I haven't heard from the firm.
5. Do not attempt to access, scan, or interact with the test environment yourself, and do not contact the firm on my behalf without my review.

When done, report back: the tracker entry created/updated, the drafted status-check message, and the checkpoint date you've noted. Clearly state that the actual testing activity remains a human step handled by the third-party firm, and that your role here was limited to preparing tracking and follow-up materials, not performing or verifying the test itself.

comp_013:n5.prompt:
You are helping me triage this year's pentest findings into our {{vendor}} project-management tracker before the retest cycle begins. If you don't have them, ask me for: (1) the pentest findings report or list (title, description, severity, affected asset/component for each finding), (2) our {{vendor}} workspace/team or project identifier where security issues should live, (3) our severity-to-priority mapping convention, (4) the engineer(s) or team to assign findings to, and (5) our SLA/due-date policy per severity (e.g., criticals in 7 days, highs in 30 days).

Once you have these, using {{vendor}}'s documented public API (e.g., an issue-creation mutation like IssueCreate), create one tracked issue per finding with: title summarizing the vulnerability, full description/repro details from the report, a severity label matching our mapping, the correct project/team, an assignee, and a due date derived from our SLA policy. If {{vendor}} supports custom fields or workflow statuses, set a 'Security Finding' or equivalent status/field so these are filterable separately from regular work. If {{vendor}} supports automation rules, set up (or confirm existing) rules so future findings of a given severity auto-route to the right assignee/queue, and if AI-based triage/prioritization is available, enable or verify it against our mapping.

Done looks like: every finding from the report has a corresponding tracked issue with severity label, assignee, and due date, all issues are queryable in one view/filter for our SOC 2 auditor and trust center evidence, and any automation rules are active for next year's cycle.

Report back: a list of created issue IDs/links mapped to original finding titles, the severity breakdown, and confirmation of any automation rules configured.

comp_013:n6.prompt:
You are helping me remediate the critical and high findings from this year's penetration test before we can request the retest from the pen test firm. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: (a) the pen test findings report or list of findings (file, PDF, or exported CSV), (b) the name of the issue tracker we use (e.g. Jira, Linear, GitHub Issues, Asana) and confirmation you have configured access to it, and (c) the name of our trust center or SOC 2 evidence folder if findings need to be logged there too.

2. From the findings report, extract every finding rated Critical or High. For each, capture: title, severity, affected asset/system, description, and the firm's recommended remediation.

3. Create or update a ticket in our issue tracker for each critical/high finding, using consistent naming (e.g. "PenTest-2025: [severity] [short title]"), tagging it appropriately (security, pentest, compliance) and setting priority based on severity.

4. Where the fix is a configuration or code change I can identify a clear owner for, draft the remediation plan or pull request description with the specific change needed (e.g. patch version, config setting, access control fix) based on the report's recommendation — but do not merge or deploy changes yourself unless I've explicitly told you that you have deployment authority for this environment.

5. Track status of each ticket until it is marked resolved, and compile a remediation summary listing: finding, severity, status (fixed/in progress/blocked), owner, and date closed.

Done looks like: every critical and high finding has a corresponding tracked ticket, a documented remediation action, and a status. Report back to me with the full list of findings, their current status, and the remediation summary, so I can confirm we're ready to request the retest letter.

comp_013:n7.prompt:
You are helping me close out our annual penetration test by requesting the retest and formal attestation letter from the firm that performed the test. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the pen-test firm's name and how we communicate with them (client portal login details I'll provide access to, or the contact email/support form), (2) the list or tracker link of findings we've remediated (especially all criticals/highs), and (3) where our trust center or compliance repository lives so you know where the letter needs to end up.

Once you have this, do the following: draft a clear, professional retest request message referencing our engagement/project ID (ask me if unknown), listing each remediated finding by ID/title and stating it is ready for verification, and asking them to (a) perform the retest and (b) issue the formal attestation/retest letter confirming remediation status for our SOC 2 auditors and customers. Include a requested turnaround date if I give you one.

Send this via the vendor's client portal or their email/support form using your configured credentials or my logged-in session. After sending, monitor for their response and the delivered retest results and attestation letter. When the letter arrives, save it and update our findings tracker to mark each retested item as verified-closed, noting the retest date and letter reference.

Report back with: the date the request was sent, the channel used, the firm's response/status, and confirmation once the attestation letter is received and filed, including where it's stored for trust center use.
